package_info.package_versions: Ubuntu: <=0.105-26ubuntu1.1, Debian: <=0.105-31, CentOS/Fedora/RHEL: all versions prior to vendor patch (see advisories)
package_info.why_malicious: The pkexec binary in PolicyKit is vulnerable to a local privilege escalation (CVE-2021-4034, 'PwnKit') that allows unprivileged users to execute arbitrary code as root by manipulating environment variables, leading to arbitrary library loading and root access.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code sets the SHELL environment variable to the path of an attacker-controlled .so file and executes pkexec, causing pkexec to load and execute the attacker's shared library as root.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Setting environment variables to point to attacker-controlled shared objects and executing a SUID-root binary is a classic privilege escalation technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, pkexec should not allow unprivileged users to load arbitrary libraries or execute code as root based on environment variables.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of pkexec would involve invoking it to run authorized commands as root, not to load arbitrary shared objects.
key_indicators: SHELL environment variable set to a .so file

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code sets the CHARSET environment variable to the path of an attacker-controlled .so file and executes pkexec, causing pkexec to load and execute the attacker's shared library as root.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Manipulating the CHARSET environment variable to point to a malicious shared object is not a normal use case and is indicative of exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: pkexec should not interpret environment variables in a way that allows arbitrary code execution as root.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: CHARSET is sometimes used to specify character encoding, but never as a path to a shared object.
key_indicators: CHARSET environment variable set to a .so file

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code sets the PATH environment variable to include a directory containing an attacker-controlled .so file and executes pkexec, causing pkexec to load and execute the attacker's shared library as root.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Altering the PATH environment variable to include a malicious shared object for a SUID-root binary is a known privilege escalation vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: PATH should be used to locate executables, not to load arbitrary shared objects as root.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PATH is legitimately used to control command lookup, but not for shared object injection.
key_indicators: PATH environment variable manipulated to include attacker-controlled directory

attack_chain.action: Attacker crafts a malicious shared object (.so) file containing code to be executed as root.
Attacker sets environment variables (SHELL, CHARSET, or PATH) to reference the malicious .so file and executes pkexec.
attack_chain.leads_to: pkexec loads and executes the attacker's code as root

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in the .so file runs with root privileges, allowing privilege escalation or further compromise.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of /usr/bin/pkexec by non-root users with unusual environment variables (SHELL, CHARSET, PATH) set
pkexec process spawning with environment variables referencing .so files or non-standard values
Unexpected shared object loading by pkexec
file_indicators: Presence of attacker-controlled .so files in user-writable directories
network_indicators: None inherent to exploit, but post-exploitation activity may include outbound connections from root processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor executions of /usr/bin/pkexec by non-root users, especially when the environment variables SHELL, CHARSET, or PATH are set to suspicious values (such as paths to .so files or non-standard directories). Alert on pkexec processes with these environment variables present, and investigate any shared object files in user-writable locations. Use EDR or kernel-level monitoring to detect abnormal privilege escalations and SUID binary abuse.
